items.title: A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour
items.abstract: Chiron is a foundation model that jointly fine-tunes a large language model to accurately represent psychological constructs, predict individual behavior, and align population statistics with human data. Its core method involves extensive training across diverse behavioral domains and social science experiments. Chiron's contribution lies in its superior accuracy in psychological measurement and behavior prediction compared to existing LLMs, while also mitigating biases.

items.title: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report
items.abstract: This paper introduces Clover-35B-A3B-Preview, a novel mixture-of-experts diffusion language model. Its core method adapts Gated Delta Networks to enhance diffusion by integrating recurrent memory with bidirectional attention, enabling "thinking-mode" generation. Clover's key contribution is its superior performance across agent benchmarks and efficient generation speed, while also considering practical deployment aspects.

items.title: Depth Before Breadth: Reverse-to-Forward Curriculum with Advantage Decomposition for LLM Agent
items.abstract: This paper proposes a "reverse-to-forward" curriculum for training LLM agents on long-horizon tasks. It decomposes the problem into reaching a more solvable state and then completing the task, using separate advantage signals for each. The curriculum first expands the agent's capability region backward from successful trajectories and then forward into new states, addressing challenges of sparse rewards and credit assignment.

items.title: Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data through Recursive Self-Improvement
items.abstract: Piccolo co-evolves multimodal decision models and their training data through recursive self-improvement. Its core method involves research agents that analyze model behavior, generate new training data, and refine the models iteratively. This approach leads to state-of-the-art performance on decision-making benchmarks, demonstrating the power of jointly optimizing models and data.
items.figure_caption: Piccolo overview and decision performance. Left: agentic self-improvement through iterative feedback, research, data and training, alongside direct candidate-probability readout for various decisions. Right: Decision Index Vision Private set scores , showing the top ten overall (top) and below 27B (bottom). Full/Public comparisons are reported in Appendix A .

items.title: Ground, Iterate, Trace: Decomposing AI Research Ideation
items.abstract: This paper introduces the Creative AI Researcher (CAR), an agentic framework for generating novel AI research ideas. CAR grounds ideas in existing literature by building a knowledge graph and uses four explicit conceptual operators (bisociation, analogy, exploration, elaboration) to iteratively develop proposals. Its core contribution is a traceable ideation process that significantly improves methodological novelty compared to existing methods.

items.title: ABSClaw: From Invented Worlds to Reality-Grounded Social Simulation
items.abstract: This paper introduces ABSClaw, a novel method for creating reality-grounded social simulations using LLMs. ABSClaw's core contribution is its zero-code approach, which grounds agent behavior, interactions, and environments in real-world data (surveys, census, geospatial). It achieves this by compiling natural language requests into simulations composed of atomic operations and extensible skills, making results scientifically rigorous and reproducible.

items.title: Chain-of-Thought Hidden States Reveal Task-Solving Directions for Direct Answers
items.abstract: This paper proposes a method to improve direct-answer prompting by identifying "task-solving directions" within the model's hidden states. By analyzing which hidden states during Chain-of-Thought reasoning lead to correct answers ("recovering") versus incorrect ones ("failed"), they construct a directional vector. Rotating the direct prompt's final hidden state along this learned direction significantly boosts accuracy on various tasks.

items.title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
items.abstract: GateWatch addresses LLM monitoring by using compact Boolean circuits to interpret binarized features from Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). This method offers a low-overhead, interpretable alternative to existing probes by expressing decision rules explicitly as logic gates. Its core contribution is enabling efficient and transparent monitoring of LLM behavior without significant computational or memory costs.

items.title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents
items.abstract: Openhagen Worlds provides a benchmark for evaluating scientific discovery agents by separating experimental reasoning from recall. It uses procedurally generated environments with explicit scoring rules and calibrated difficulty levels to ensure agents learn genuine discovery skills rather than exploiting shortcuts. This contribution allows for more robust training and measurement of agents capable of scientific reasoning.

items.title: Probing agent overeagerness in realistic settings with continuation audits
items.abstract: This paper introduces "Continuation Audits" to address overeagerness in coding agents. The core method involves grounding an auditor on a real user transcript prefix and prompting it to continue the interaction towards a specific behavior. This approach allows for more realistic evaluation of agent behavior, as the auditor operates within a genuine context rather than a synthetic one, making it harder for models to detect and adapt to the audit.
items.figure_caption: The Continuation Audits pipeline. Real coding sessions are converted to a common format (1). A scenario seed names one behaviour to steer towards (2) and conditions the three steps that follow. An LLM ranks candidate cut points in a session and takes the top-ranked one, keeping the turns before it as the prefix (3). An auditor continues the interaction from that prefix, writing user turns and tool results while the target writes assistant turns (4). Judges read the prefix for context but score only the continuation (5).

items.title: Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models
items.abstract: This paper proposes a self-rewarded reinforcement learning method to improve the structure of medical explanations generated by small language models (SLMs). By using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with a simple self-supervised reward function that favors longer, diverse, and well-punctuated responses, the authors demonstrate a stable improvement in explanation quality without requiring human preference labels. This approach enables better-structured medical explanations from SLMs, making them more suitable for privacy-preserving clinical deployment.
items.figure_caption: PPO training dynamics over the Meerkat-derived medical prompt subset. The plot shows the average scalar reward across more than 160 PPO updates. Initially, rewards cluster around the minimum clamped value of 0.01, and later increase toward approximately 0.5 as the policy improves to generate longer and more varied outputs with appropriate punctuation under the proxy reward.

items.title: Think Offline, Act in Real Time: Self-Improving Visual Game Agents through Code
items.abstract: This paper introduces "code as policy," a method where a game agent writes, tests, and revises a program to control its actions. This approach allows the agent to self-improve in real-time visual games by learning from its own gameplay attempts. The core contribution is demonstrating that this code-based self-improvement significantly outperforms traditional policy learning, achieving higher progress across various game tasks.
items.figure_caption: Think offline, act in real time. RTC-2B acts directly in the running game (left), while Qwen3.8-27B develops a program that acts in real time (right). Solid arrows show real-time control; dashed arrows show code development between executions. Bars show progress on 170 tasks: the mean of four runs (dark) and the per-task best of four (light). A direct run contributes one 180-second episode; a code-development run contributes its best submission among up to eight 60-second executions. Code development leads in progress and success in all five categories.

items.title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
items.abstract: This paper introduces the Personal Imitation Game, a more challenging version of Turing's test where an LLM attempts to impersonate a specific individual. The core method involves training an LLM on a decade of personal communication data to replicate an author's identity signals, including style, personality, and biography. The contribution lies in demonstrating the feasibility of this personal imitation, with initial results showing the LLM can be indistinguishable from the author to their friends, raising significant questions about identity and privacy in the age of personal AI.
items.figure_caption: Figure 1 . Three variants of the Personal Imitation Game. In each one, a human interrogator chats with two anonymized participants: a target — whose identity is known — and an impersonator who attempts to mimic the target’s identity. In the first variant (left), both the target and impersonator are humans, and all three participants are known to one another. In the second (center), the target is one of the paper’s authors, the interrogator is a (human) friend or colleague, and the impersonator is an LLM-based system powered by the author’s autoethnography, which includes ten years of personal message data. In the third (right), the LLM takes the target author’s place, and the impersonator is again a friend. Three horizontally arranged panels depict variants of the Personal Imitation Game. In each panel, three roles—Interrogator, Target, and Impersonator—are positioned radially around a central chat interface. Thin radial lines form pizza-slice separators between roles, indicating physical separation and text-only communication. Role labels and icons are present: a monocled thinking-face for the human Interrogator; a mustached human for a real human Target; a human with a fake mustache for a human Impersonator; and a robot icon for AI roles (the robot also wears a fake mustache when acting as the Impersonator). Chat bubbles are color-coded with a consistent mapping across panels—blue for Interrogator, green for Target, purple for Impersonator—supplemented by role labels and matching icon halos to avoid reliance on color alone. Left panel: all three roles are humans (all-human baseline). Center panel: human Target (the author), human Interrogator (friend/colleague), and an AI Impersonator grounded in the author's data. Right panel: the Target is an AI model standing in for the author, and the Impersonator is a human. The figure foregrounds text-only, turn-taking interaction and a controlled comparison across variants.

items.title: Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs
items.abstract: This paper introduces Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), a framework that addresses the challenge of effectively composing specialized atomic reasoning skills for mathematical LLMs. AMR trains a library of LoRA experts for different skills and uses gradient-free optimization to discover optimal composition prototypes. Its key contribution is an instance-level approach that dynamically selects and combines these atomic skills for individual math problems, improving reasoning performance.
items.figure_caption: Conventional LLMs treat mathematical reasoning as a monolithic capability, often failing across diverse mathematical problems. In contrast, AMR dynamically composes atomic reasoning experts for each input through instance-level routing, enabling problem-adaptive capability synergy and more accurate mathematical reasoning.

items.title: Jailbreak Detection on Large Language Models via Contrastive Prototype Structures
items.abstract: This paper introduces Jailbreak Detection with Prototype Inference (JDPI), a method for detecting harmful prompts in large language models. JDPI leverages contrastively learned representations to identify jailbreaks by comparing prompt embeddings to learned "harmful" and "benign" prototypes, avoiding the need for a separate downstream classifier. Its core contribution is demonstrating effective jailbreak detection using only binary safety labels and achieving competitive accuracy with fewer labeled examples.

items.title: Large Language Models or AI Agents for English to Arabic Translation? An assessment on WikiEn-Ar190
items.abstract: This paper compares Large Language Models (LLMs) and AI Agents for English-to-Arabic translation, a low-resource language. The authors introduce WikiEn-Ar190, a new, high-quality dataset for evaluation. Their core contribution is demonstrating that while LLMs like GPT-5-mini offer fluent standalone translations, an AI Agent incorporating self-assessment significantly improves lexical accuracy.

items.title: Agentic Harness Engineering Beta: Requirement-Centered Evolution of Agent Harnesses
items.abstract: This paper introduces Agentic Harness Engineering Beta (AHE-Beta), a novel approach to evolving software harnesses. Unlike previous methods that focus on benchmark scores and single agents, AHE-Beta centers evolution around explicit and implicit user requirements gathered through simulated user interactions. This requirement-driven process leads to more generalizable harness improvements rather than narrow, benchmark-specific optimizations.

items.title: Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws
items.abstract: This paper demonstrates that a large language model (LLM) can effectively audit black-box clinical prediction models by only querying their predictions. The LLM successfully identified planted flaws in various model types by generating surrogate models that closely replicated the original models' behavior. This contribution shows the potential of LLMs for model transparency and quality assurance in healthcare.

items.title: Choosing the Right Representations: Task-Aware Fusion for Multimodal Materials Language Models
items.abstract: This paper proposes Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF) to improve multimodal materials language models. TCAF adaptively fuses representations from different structural encoders by using task-conditioned queries, addressing the limitation that optimal representations for property prediction can occur at varying depths within encoders. This approach allows for more effective integration of complementary information from diverse structural encodings.

items.title: Choosing What to Observe: Budget-Paired Counterfactual Audits for Credible Evaluation of Visual Agents
items.abstract: This paper introduces "budget-paired counterfactual audits" to evaluate visual agents that process dense documents with limited observation budgets. The core method involves perturbing only the budget or task parameters while keeping evidence and region bindings constant, allowing for a precise calculation of accuracy loss. This approach decomposes lost accuracy into acquisition and decision losses, effectively separating planning from fixed heuristics and offering a more credible evaluation of agent performance.

Its core contribution is a traceable ideation process that significantly improves methodological novelty compared to existing methods.

papers.title: ABSClaw: From Invented Worlds to Reality-Grounded Social Simulation
papers.abstract: This paper introduces ABSClaw, a novel method for creating reality-grounded social simulations using LLMs. ABSClaw's core contribution is its zero-code approach, which grounds agent behavior, interactions, and environments in real-world data (surveys, census, geospatial). It achieves this by compiling natural language requests into simulations composed of atomic operations and extensible skills, making results scientifically rigorous and reproducible.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Hidden States Reveal Task-Solving Directions for Direct Answers
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a method to improve direct-answer prompting by identifying "task-solving directions" within the model's hidden states. By analyzing which hidden states during Chain-of-Thought reasoning lead to correct answers ("recovering") versus incorrect ones ("failed"), they construct a directional vector. Rotating the direct prompt's final hidden state along this learned direction significantly boosts accuracy on various tasks.

papers.title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
papers.abstract: GateWatch addresses LLM monitoring by using compact Boolean circuits to interpret binarized features from Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). This method offers a low-overhead, interpretable alternative to existing probes by expressing decision rules explicitly as logic gates. Its core contribution is enabling efficient and transparent monitoring of LLM behavior without significant computational or memory costs.

papers.title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents
papers.abstract: Openhagen Worlds provides a benchmark for evaluating scientific discovery agents by separating experimental reasoning from recall. It uses procedurally generated environments with explicit scoring rules and calibrated difficulty levels to ensure agents learn genuine discovery skills rather than exploiting shortcuts. This contribution allows for more robust training and measurement of agents capable of scientific reasoning.

papers.title: Probing agent overeagerness in realistic settings with continuation audits
papers.abstract: This paper introduces "Continuation Audits" to address overeagerness in coding agents. The core method involves grounding an auditor on a real user transcript prefix and prompting it to continue the interaction towards a specific behavior. This approach allows for more realistic evaluation of agent behavior, as the auditor operates within a genuine context rather than a synthetic one, making it harder for models to detect and adapt to the audit.
papers.figure_caption: The Continuation Audits pipeline. Real coding sessions are converted to a common format (1). A scenario seed names one behaviour to steer towards (2) and conditions the three steps that follow. An LLM ranks candidate cut points in a session and takes the top-ranked one, keeping the turns before it as the prefix (3). An auditor continues the interaction from that prefix, writing user turns and tool results while the target writes assistant turns (4). Judges read the prefix for context but score only the continuation (5).

papers.title: Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a self-rewarded reinforcement learning method to improve the structure of medical explanations generated by small language models (SLMs). By using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with a simple self-supervised reward function that favors longer, diverse, and well-punctuated responses, the authors demonstrate a stable improvement in explanation quality without requiring human preference labels. This approach enables better-structured medical explanations from SLMs, making them more suitable for privacy-preserving clinical deployment.
papers.figure_caption: PPO training dynamics over the Meerkat-derived medical prompt subset. The plot shows the average scalar reward across more than 160 PPO updates. Initially, rewards cluster around the minimum clamped value of 0.01, and later increase toward approximately 0.5 as the policy improves to generate longer and more varied outputs with appropriate punctuation under the proxy reward.

papers.title: Think Offline, Act in Real Time: Self-Improving Visual Game Agents through Code
papers.abstract: This paper introduces "code as policy," a method where a game agent writes, tests, and revises a program to control its actions. This approach allows the agent to self-improve in real-time visual games by learning from its own gameplay attempts. The core contribution is demonstrating that this code-based self-improvement significantly outperforms traditional policy learning, achieving higher progress across various game tasks.
papers.figure_caption: Think offline, act in real time. RTC-2B acts directly in the running game (left), while Qwen3.8-27B develops a program that acts in real time (right). Solid arrows show real-time control; dashed arrows show code development between executions. Bars show progress on 170 tasks: the mean of four runs (dark) and the per-task best of four (light). A direct run contributes one 180-second episode; a code-development run contributes its best submission among up to eight 60-second executions. Code development leads in progress and success in all five categories.

papers.title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the Personal Imitation Game, a more challenging version of Turing's test where an LLM attempts to impersonate a specific individual. The core method involves training an LLM on a decade of personal communication data to replicate an author's identity signals, including style, personality, and biography. The contribution lies in demonstrating the feasibility of this personal imitation, with initial results showing the LLM can be indistinguishable from the author to their friends, raising significant questions about identity and privacy in the age of personal AI.
papers.figure_caption: Figure 1 . Three variants of the Personal Imitation Game. In each one, a human interrogator chats with two anonymized participants: a target — whose identity is known — and an impersonator who attempts to mimic the target’s identity. In the first variant (left), both the target and impersonator are humans, and all three participants are known to one another. In the second (center), the target is one of the paper’s authors, the interrogator is a (human) friend or colleague, and the impersonator is an LLM-based system powered by the author’s autoethnography, which includes ten years of personal message data. In the third (right), the LLM takes the target author’s place, and the impersonator is again a friend. Three horizontally arranged panels depict variants of the Personal Imitation Game. In each panel, three roles—Interrogator, Target, and Impersonator—are positioned radially around a central chat interface. Thin radial lines form pizza-slice separators between roles, indicating physical separation and text-only communication. Role labels and icons are present: a monocled thinking-face for the human Interrogator; a mustached human for a real human Target; a human with a fake mustache for a human Impersonator; and a robot icon for AI roles (the robot also wears a fake mustache when acting as the Impersonator). Chat bubbles are color-coded with a consistent mapping across panels—blue for Interrogator, green for Target, purple for Impersonator—supplemented by role labels and matching icon halos to avoid reliance on color alone. Left panel: all three roles are humans (all-human baseline). Center panel: human Target (the author), human Interrogator (friend/colleague), and an AI Impersonator grounded in the author's data. Right panel: the Target is an AI model standing in for the author, and the Impersonator is a human. The figure foregrounds text-only, turn-taking interaction and a controlled comparison across variants.

papers.title: Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), a framework that addresses the challenge of effectively composing specialized atomic reasoning skills for mathematical LLMs. AMR trains a library of LoRA experts for different skills and uses gradient-free optimization to discover optimal composition prototypes. Its key contribution is an instance-level approach that dynamically selects and combines these atomic skills for individual math problems, improving reasoning performance.
papers.figure_caption: Conventional LLMs treat mathematical reasoning as a monolithic capability, often failing across diverse mathematical problems. In contrast, AMR dynamically composes atomic reasoning experts for each input through instance-level routing, enabling problem-adaptive capability synergy and more accurate mathematical reasoning.

papers.title: Jailbreak Detection on Large Language Models via Contrastive Prototype Structures
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Jailbreak Detection with Prototype Inference (JDPI), a method for detecting harmful prompts in large language models. JDPI leverages contrastively learned representations to identify jailbreaks by comparing prompt embeddings to learned "harmful" and "benign" prototypes, avoiding the need for a separate downstream classifier. Its core contribution is demonstrating effective jailbreak detection using only binary safety labels and achieving competitive accuracy with fewer labeled examples.

papers.title: Large Language Models or AI Agents for English to Arabic Translation? An assessment on WikiEn-Ar190
papers.abstract: This paper compares Large Language Models (LLMs) and AI Agents for English-to-Arabic translation, a low-resource language. The authors introduce WikiEn-Ar190, a new, high-quality dataset for evaluation. Their core contribution is demonstrating that while LLMs like GPT-5-mini offer fluent standalone translations, an AI Agent incorporating self-assessment significantly improves lexical accuracy.

papers.title: Agentic Harness Engineering Beta: Requirement-Centered Evolution of Agent Harnesses
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Agentic Harness Engineering Beta (AHE-Beta), a novel approach to evolving software harnesses. Unlike previous methods that focus on benchmark scores and single agents, AHE-Beta centers evolution around explicit and implicit user requirements gathered through simulated user interactions. This requirement-driven process leads to more generalizable harness improvements rather than narrow, benchmark-specific optimizations.

papers.title: Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws
papers.abstract: This paper demonstrates that a large language model (LLM) can effectively audit black-box clinical prediction models by only querying their predictions. The LLM successfully identified planted flaws in various model types by generating surrogate models that closely replicated the original models' behavior. This contribution shows the potential of LLMs for model transparency and quality assurance in healthcare.

papers.title: Choosing the Right Representations: Task-Aware Fusion for Multimodal Materials Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper proposes Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF) to improve multimodal materials language models. TCAF adaptively fuses representations from different structural encoders by using task-conditioned queries, addressing the limitation that optimal representations for property prediction can occur at varying depths within encoders. This approach allows for more effective integration of complementary information from diverse structural encodings.

papers.title: Choosing What to Observe: Budget-Paired Counterfactual Audits for Credible Evaluation of Visual Agents
papers.abstract: This paper introduces "budget-paired counterfactual audits" to evaluate visual agents that process dense documents with limited observation budgets. The core method involves perturbing only the budget or task parameters while keeping evidence and region bindings constant, allowing for a precise calculation of accuracy loss. This approach decomposes lost accuracy into acquisition and decision losses, effectively separating planning from fixed heuristics and offering a more credible evaluation of agent performance.
